summary: This Best Current Practice sets out how IANA should manage DNS parameter registries: resource record types, classes, opcodes, error codes, header bits, and AFSDB subtypes. It defines which registration procedures apply to each, so new values get assigned consistently. It was replaced by RFC 6895.

eli5.summary: The DNS has lists of numbers with special meanings, like which record type is which. This document says who gets to add new numbers to those lists and how. It was later replaced by RFC 6895.

subtitle: How IANA allocates DNS parameter registry values

tldr.problem: DNS uses many parameter codes: message header bits, operation codes, error codes, resource record types and classes. Without clear rules, these codes are allocated inconsistently and may be used for conflicting purposes.
tldr.mechanism: Defines allocation policies (Standards Action, IETF Review, Expert Review, etc.) for each DNS parameter space. Each code range and parameter type has explicit rules: what policy applies, whether assignments are permanent, and when IANA needs to consult experts or the IESG.
tldr.outcome: DNS can safely add new features without number collisions. The registry is transparent and extensible, and new RRTYPEs can be added with expert review rather than waiting for a full standards process.

facts.value: 4 bits; extended to 12 or 16 bits in OPT/TSIG/TKEY

today: RFC 6195 is the current Best Current Practice for DNS IANA considerations. It updates RFC 1183 and RFC 3597, and obsoletes RFC 5395 (an earlier version). It is the authoritative guide for allocating new DNS parameters, and IANA uses it to manage DNS registries.

sections.title: Overview of DNS Parameter Allocation
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) is built on protocol codes: operation codes (Query, Update, Notify), error codes (NoError, FormErr, NXDomain), message header bits, and resource record types and classes. Each code is a number from a finite space.

This memo consolidates IANA considerations for all these spaces. It replaces earlier ad-hoc allocation practices with clear, uniform rules. For each space, it specifies which allocation policy applies, which numbers are reserved, which ranges allow private use, and when approval from experts or the IESG is needed.
sections.eli5: DNS has a ledger of what each number means: 'A' records are type 1, 'AAAA' are type 28, and so on. This document says how new entries get added to that ledger and who decides.

sections.title: Header Bits and Operation Codes
sections.content:
DNS queries and responses have a 16-bit header with flags (bits that turn features on and off) and fields for operation codes and error codes.

The QR bit (bit 0) says whether it's a query or a response. The AA, TC, RD, RA, AD, CD bits control other behavior. Most have different meanings in queries and responses. The Z bit is reserved; assigning it a new meaning requires Standards Action.

Operation codes are 4-bit values (0–15). Currently: 0 is Query, 1 is obsolete IQuery, 2 is Status, 4 is Notify, 5 is Update. New codes require Standards Action. Response codes (RCODEs) can be 4, 8, 12, or 16 bits depending on where they appear. New RCODEs in available ranges require IETF Review.
sections.eli5: The header is like a command word: bit 0 says 'I'm asking' or 'I'm answering', bits 4–6 say what kind of request, and bits 8–11 say whether it worked or what went wrong. New meanings for these bits need approval.

sections.title: Resource Records and Their Types
sections.content:
A resource record (RR) is the unit of DNS data: a name, a type, a class, a TTL, and data. Types distinguish what the record is: A (IPv4 address), AAAA (IPv6), MX (mail server), CNAME (alias), and many others.

Types are 16-bit numbers (0–65535), grouped into ranges:

Data types (1–127, 256–61439, others): store actual data. Expert Review if they can be safely handled as unknown. Standards Action otherwise. Query types (255 downward, except OPT at 41): only for queries (like AXFR, transfer all records). Meta-types (like OPT, TSIG, TKEY): transient data in a message; optional processing.

Classes (like IN for Internet) are 16-bit. IN is class 1; new classes require IETF Review. Labels (parts of a domain name) can be text (ASCII and others) or binary; the Binary type is experimental.
sections.eli5: Records have types like 'A record', 'MX record'. The system says: new types can be added by expert review if they're safe to ignore, otherwise you need full standards work. Classes let you have different DNS databases for different networks.

sections.title: Registration Processes
sections.content:
Different parameters use different allocation policies:

Standards Action: requires a published RFC on the Standards Track. Most restrictive; used for core DNS features.

IETF Review: requires review and consensus by the IETF community; faster than Standards Action but still formal.

Expert Review (for RRTYPEs): a small pool of DNS experts, appointed by the IESG, review applications. The applicant posts a template, the expert reviews for 3–6 weeks, and approves or rejects. This is faster and allows experimentation.

Specification Required: the parameter must be described in a stable document.

Private Use (65280–65534 in most spaces): reserved for experimental or internal use; no registration needed.
sections.eli5: The further apart your plan is from the main DNS spec, the more approval you need. Adding a new error code needs everyone to agree. Adding a new record type can just be reviewed by experts. Experimenting privately needs no approval at all.
